message.content: Your question appears to be cut off at "putting it on" — but I'll work with what's there and address the two main questions: the Knights of Ren as a third-party breakaway, and whether a thermal-detonator-as-holocron is a character-appropriate move for Hux. The Knights of Ren are positioned in canon as a semi-autonomous faction whose loyalties are to dark-side mysticism rather than to any single political regime, making a breakaway from the First Order plausible. The Knights operate more like a cabal of dark-side sorcerers than a military unit. Their relationship with the First Order is transactional — they serve Kylo Ren and, by extension, the leadership, but they have their own goals (the hunt for the Sith Wayfinder, for instance). Snoke's death already removed the figure they were most explicitly aligned with, and Kylo Ren is more of a client than a true master. If they decided the First Order's military apparatus was too crude or too exposed to the Resistance, defecting or playing both sides would fit their self-interested, almost alchemical worldview. They're not stormtroopers; they're the equivalent of a warlock guild. A "third party" role is arguably the most *in-character* thing they could do, because it's not even a betrayal so much as a shift in whose patron they serve. Disguising a thermal detonator as a holocron is a clever piece of misdirection, but it is not a move that fits Hux's established character — it fits the Knights of Ren perfectly, which may be the more interesting reading of your scenario. Hux is a blunt, insecure, status-conscious military officer. His "scheming" in *The Last Jedi* is limited to fudging reports and trying to look competent in front of his superiors. He's not a spymaster or a trickster. If Hux were the one building the device, it would read as a significant and uncharacteristic upgrade in cunning — not impossible, but a stretch that would need heavy justification (e.g., he's desperate, cornered, and has been studying Resistance tactics). However, if you flip it — if the *Knights of Ren* set this trap on the First Order, targeting Hux specifically — it becomes almost *too* on-the-nose to be good, but it's in character. A holocron is an object of dark-side lore; the Knights would have the knowledge, the materials, and the aesthetic to craft something that looks like a genuine relic. Placing it where Hux would find it (a captured Resistance cache, a "reward" for his loyalty, a trophy from a battle) and letting his ambition make him handle it is exactly the kind of slow, elegant knife-in-the-back that fits a sorcerer faction. Hux, being the kind of person who would grab a shiny holocron to show off or to deliver to the Emperor's remnant, would be the perfect mark. The strongest version of this scenario is not Hux as the architect but Hux as the victim, with the Knights of Ren using the holocron aesthetic as a narrative trap that exploits his character flaw of craving recognition and status. That's where the cleverness lives: not in the engineering of the device, but in the *social engineering* — choosing the right person to walk into it because of who he is.
